title: Sell Mineral Rights in Bethlehem, WV
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Bethlehem, WV | Ohio County
metaDescription: Bethlehem, WV sits just outside Wheeling in Ohio County. We buy mineral and royalty interests here, including old flat-rate leases and heir shares.
heroLead: Bethlehem sits just outside Wheeling in Ohio County, close enough to the city that a lot of its mineral history is tangled up with land that was subdivided for suburban growth long after the mineral rights were already severed.
intro: Ohio County's proximity to Wheeling means Bethlehem's tracts often carry a two-part history: farmland leased for gas decades ago, then later sold off in pieces for residential development while the original family kept the minerals. That produces a mineral estate that no longer matches the current surface lot lines at all.

We buy mineral and royalty interests around Bethlehem directly, tracing the original tract description back through the deed record so the interest we're buying matches what's actually recorded, not the modern parcel map.

sections.heading: When surface development outpaces the mineral record
paragraphs: It's common in the Wheeling suburbs for a single mineral tract, described by an old metes-and-bounds survey, to now underlie a dozen residential lots. The mineral owner's interest doesn't shrink because the surface got subdivided, but proving the boundary sometimes takes real courthouse work.

sections.heading: Legacy leases from before suburban growth
paragraphs: Some Bethlehem-area leases predate the residential development entirely, written when the land was still farmland. Older leases can carry flat-rate payment terms that never converted to West Virginia's statutory one-eighth royalty minimum, which we check before pricing your interest.

sections.heading: Ohio County unit activity
paragraphs: Modern horizontal units in this part of Ohio County can pull acreage from several original farm tracts at once. If your interest sits inside an active unit, we confirm the unit order and your decimal share before naming a number.

Because Ohio County is smaller and more urbanized than its neighbors, fewer new units get formed here each year than in Marshall or Harrison County. That makes it worth checking whether an existing unit order already reaches your Bethlehem tract before assuming it's untouched.

faqs.question: My mineral tract predates the subdivision my house sits in now. How do you verify it?
faqs.answer: We trace the original metes-and-bounds description through the Ohio County deed record to confirm your interest against the historical tract, independent of the current lot lines.

faqs.question: Is my old Bethlehem-area lease still valid?
faqs.answer: Many legacy leases remain in effect as long as production or its statutory equivalent continues. We review the recorded lease and current unit status to confirm.

faqs.question: What if I only own minerals under part of my old family's land?
faqs.answer: That's common after partial sales or partitions. We identify your specific fractional share from the recorded deeds before making an offer.

faqs.question: Does a residential subdivision change who owns the minerals underneath it?
faqs.answer: No. Subdividing and selling the surface doesn't affect a previously severed mineral estate. The original mineral owner, or their heirs, still hold the same interest regardless of how the surface above it was later developed.
